extracted.intended_audience: scientists, philosophers of science, and students interested in scientific method, terminology, and classification
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for constructing and evaluating scientific/ philosophical language, terminology, nomenclature, and classification so as to support precise description, induction, and useful groupings of real objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision/definiteness in descriptive terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an exact and extensive descriptive language to record observations of outward objects; only impressions connected uniformly with outward objects admit precise description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes the high degree of precision attainable in sciences handling external objects (example: botany). Include specific terms for every part and fine distinctions (e.g., calyx, corolla, pinnatifid, bifid), and avoid attempting precise naming for subjective sensations that cannot be shared among observers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology for properties and standardized scales
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt standardized descriptive terms and measurable scales for important properties (color, hardness, specific gravity, crystalline form) so properties can be conveyed precisely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Werner's classified color scale; Mohs numerical hardness scale (talc=1, gypsum=2, etc.); use numerical measures where definition admits (specific gravity) and mathematical reasoning for structural properties (crystalline form).

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise names for newly abstracted general conceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever comparison of phenomena yields a new general conception, assign it a concise term to fix attention and facilitate reasoning and memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short, compact names (e.g., 'limit', 'momentum', 'delegation') make complex ideas available to thought, aid retention, and speed discovery. The naming is not merely shorthand but helps concentrate intellectual effort on relations rather than verbose definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomenclature: give names for every Kind (infima species)
rubrics_metrics.description: A systematic nomenclature should provide a name for each lowest Kind (those frequently predicated about), so future predicates and reasoning can be applied efficiently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful examples are Linnaean plant/animal nomenclature and chemical nomenclature. When new lowest Kinds are discovered, names should be assigned on a uniform principle; lacking such a system (e.g., mineralogy) hinders progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish terminology from nomenclature
rubrics_metrics.description: Terminology consists of descriptive expressions that connote attributes; nomenclature consists of names that denote Kinds (classes) and indicate an intention to denote an infima species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'linear', 'serrated' are terminology; 'Viola odorata' or 'Ulex Europaeus' are nomenclature. Treat the two differently when constructing scientific language and reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Names in a nomenclature must connote both attributes and the status of being a Kind
rubrics_metrics.description: A nomenclatural name connotes (1) certain attributes/characters and (2) that those attributes are distinctive of a Kind; the full meaning is conveyed by the definition plus the form of the word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: 'peroxide of iron' connotes composition and that it is a distinct Kind; 'Viola odorata' is defined by characters but also signals 'infima species'. If subsequent knowledge splits a formerly single Kind into several, the application of the name is revised accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic uniform principles for naming new Kinds
rubrics_metrics.description: When assigning names to newly discovered lowest Kinds, follow a uniform, systematic principle so the nomenclature remains coherent and useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Botany and chemistry assign names uniformly upon discovery; absence of a systematic principle (as in mineralogy historically) is cited as a principal reason for retardation of a science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design language to permit mechanical reasoning only where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: If the subject permits safe, mechanical manipulation of symbols (as in algebra/calculus), construct language to exploit mechanical procedures; where it does not, design language to resist purely mechanical use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algebraic symbols are ideal for domains reducible to numerical relations because they function as counters devoid of independent meaning. For non-mathematical sciences, over-symbolization is dangerous: it can lead to unconscious symbol-manipulation divorced from the phenomena, producing misapplied conclusions. Thus language should either enable mechanical operation (where valid) or actively preserve semantic content to force users to attend to meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep semantic content in words (use derivation and analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Form words so that derivation and analogy reinforce their meaning; embed as much meaning as possible in the word-formation itself to keep users conscious of what terms signify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Languages that form compounds from native roots with fixed analogies (e.g., German, Greek) better preserve meaning than those formed from foreign/downrooted elements (English, French, Italian). Prefer morphological transparency to help users recall and keep alive the concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain continual acquaintance with phenomena, not formulas alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientists should habitually contemplate the real phenomena behind formulas to prevent words/formulæ from losing their meaning and to ensure correct application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: living exclusively among formulæ and applying them without checking for counteracting laws leads to practical failure and progressive semantic decay. Regularly 'stamp afresh' the meaning of terms by direct engagement with the phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification should be organized to aid induction and discovery of laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct classifications (groups and their order) to best conduce to remembrance and to the ascertainment of general laws; naming should conform to the classificatory scheme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification is a contrivance to order ideas so that useful predicates and propositions naturally apply to groups. The principal test is the number and importance of properties that can be asserted in common of members of a group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer properties that are causes or sure marks when choosing classificatory bases
rubrics_metrics.description: Select classification properties that are causes of many other properties, or at least sure marks of them, because such bases yield groups with many shared, important consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the causal property isn't diagnosable directly, choose prominent effects that reliably indicate the cause. The goal is to form 'natural' rather than merely convenient or superficial groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification must be global in scope and consider all affinities
rubrics_metrics.description: To constitute proper scientific classes, groupings must be made with reference to all real existing objects and their affinities; families and higher arrangements are interdependent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You cannot properly define a family (e.g., of plants) except as part of a systematic arrangement of all related objects; the placement of a single object depends on comparison with all varieties having affinity to it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid artificial/technical classifications that mislead thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid basing classifications on arbitrarily selected, superficially simple properties if such groupings cause dissimilar objects to be thought together and obstruct the discovery/use of more important common properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Tournefort's corolla-shape classification or the Linnæan system based on number of stamens/pistils are helpful for certain facts (easy identification) but may be 'mischievous' if they prevent habitually thinking in groups with more significant shared properties.
